newsitem.title: GERMANY: German yield curve hammered out by mark, rate woes.
newsitem.headline: German yield curve hammered out by mark, rate woes.

text.p: The German yield curve has flattened dramatically in recent sessions, hammered out by sharp declines in the deutschemark and worries that a move to tighten short-term rates might be on the cards.

With the mark tumbling to its lowest point in 92 months at 1.8465 to the dollar in Tokyo on Monday and as yet finding little real support from its home team, curve flattening, while likely to temper in pace, is still the order of the day.
Market analysts witnessing very heavy selling pressure at the front end of the curve say the action represents some of the most impressive seen this year in the German debt market.

"What we are talking about is the yield curve flattening dramatically and accelerating in the flattening process," said David Sneddon, vice president of fixed income at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

The yield curve, which reflects the progression of interest rate expectations from three months to 30 years ahead, is flattening as markets bet that interest rates will head higher sooner, while their expectations for rates in 10 years' time have been scaled back or remain the same.

German December three-month interest rate futures, or euromarks, were trading on London's LIFFE at 96.51 by 0914 GMT on Monday -- pricing in a 40 basis point rise in three-month deposit rates by the end of the year.
At the middle of last week, the market's pricing reflected expectations of three-month market rates moving up by only half that much by December from their current 3.09 percent.
Analysts at MMS International said the technical picture in December euromarks shows a "head and shoulders" pattern with a so-called "neckline" at 96.61.

With this already line broken, a move which can signal a sharp downturn ahead, they pointed to a downside target of 96.41 for December euromarks -- another 10 basis points below current prices and a level not seen for almost five months.
In the cash market, the spread between two and 10-year debt yields squeezed in 174 basis points last week and is expected to tightening even further as investors dump short-term paper.
Yields on 10-year cash Bunds were 5.6 percent on Monday.
Charles Diebel, senior fixed income analyst at Technical Data in London, said that gap would slim to as little as 165 basis points in coming weeks.
"While the mark remains weak, there are going to be continued concerns at the short end of the curve that the Bundesbank will be forced to put rates up," he said.
"And for the moment I can't see anything that will reverse the current strong-dollar/weak-mark trend."
The weak mark, while helpful for German exporters who see their goods becoming more attractive to foreign buyers, can also pose a risk to inflation as the price of importing goods to Germany goes up.

As a result, the short end of the market is demonstrating clear concern that the Bundesbank might take at least a symbolic step to support of the mark by switching back to a variable repo rate at the next tender.

Under the fixed rate system -- which the Bundesbank has kept in place at 3.0 percent for almost a year, the central bank allocates fund at a pre-defined rate, while under a variable rate tender, banks bid for funds at different rates.

The Bundesbank fanned more speculation last week when it fixed its repurchase rate at 3.0 percent for just two weeks despite facing a four-week holiday, leaving itself the option to change to a variable rate or even to tighten the repo if developments demanded it in the final two holiday weeks.

"If the exchange rate falls significantly further in the next few weeks -- for example close to 1.90 marks to the dollar -- the Bundesbank will probably switch to a variable repurchase agreement rate and allow call money rates to rise," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers.
With that decision still open until at the latest August 12, speculation alone will drive yields on short-term paper yet higher in the coming weeks, analysts said.

The long end of the market -- which is less sensitive to near-term interest rate worries -- should remain relatively shielded from the impact of currency weakness, but at the same time will find it hard to move higher amid such uncertainty.
"What we're going to see now is an accelerated curve flattening phase with the long-end neutral to bearish and the short end increasingly bearish," said Sneddon.
